root.note: ek- ‘out’ + kaleîn ‘to call’: people called out to meet. In Athens, the assembly of citizens.

history: A church began as a political meeting. In ancient Athens the ekklēsía was the assembly of citizens, called out to discuss public affairs. Saint Paul used the word for the community of Christian believers, and Latin borrowed it as ecclēsia. Only later did it also mean the building. Spanish wore it down through Old Spanish eglesia, recorded from the 800s, to iglesia, while learned words kept the Latin look: eclesiástico, ‘of the clergy’. The Greek verb inside it, kaleîn, ‘to call’, is linked to the same old root as Latin calare, and through that to Spanish calendario. French église, Italian chiesa and Portuguese igreja all come from the Latin word, worn down in their own ways, so Spanish is in good company.
historyEinfach: Iglesia means ‘church’. The word comes from Greek. In old Athens, the ekklēsía was a meeting of citizens. They talked about the city. Later, Christians used the word for their group of believers, and then for their building. Latin took it from Greek, and it slowly became iglesia in Spanish.

elsewhere.text: French église keeps the Greek word's opening sounds better than Spanish does.
Hard to spot, but Italian chiesa is the same word, having lost its first syllable.
Portuguese igreja is the closest relative of iglesia.
